characteristics.cultivar: Qingxin Da Mao (a variety favored by tea jassids)

description.short: Unique oolong whose rich honey-fruity flavor is triggered by the bites of tiny tea leafhoppers — a one-of-a-kind natural wonder
description.overview: The only tea where the feeding of an insect (the tea jassid Jacobiasca formosana) is an indispensable prerequisite for its signature aroma — the plant's defense response produces aromatic monoterpenes and honey sweetness.
description.leaf: Striking five-colored leaf: white downy tips, silver, jade green, red, and deep brown tones
description.liquor: Rich amber-orange liquor reminiscent of black tea
description.aroma: Ripe peach, muscatel grape, wild honey, and floral undertones
description.taste: Lush, honeyed, velvety body combining the depth of black tea with the airy elegance of oolong
description.processing: Harvest of bitten leaves from pesticide-free fields → heavy solar withering → vigorous indoor tossing for deep oxidation → fixation → cloth-sack rolling → drying

history.origin: According to lore, an impoverished farmer whose crop was ravaged by insects processed the damaged leaves anyway, only to discover an astonishingly sweet, honeyed tea that sold for a fortune.
history.development: The name 'Oriental Beauty' is traditionally said to have been bestowed by Queen Victoria upon tasting the tea in England, though historian accounts vary.
history.modern: To craft authentic Bai Hao Oolong, farmers deliberately eschew pesticides to cultivate healthy jassid colonies — a remarkable case where a vineyard 'pest' becomes the key to artisanal luxury.
interestingFacts: Locally known as 'Peng Feng Cha' ('Braggart's Tea'), named because nobody believed the humble farmer when he claimed how much money merchants paid for insect-bitten leaves.
A similar insect-induced defense reaction contributes to the muscatel character in summer second-flush Darjeeling, uniting two distinct tea traditions.
